items.label: text
items.text: You can measure the amount of heat energy taken in or released in a chemical reaction. It is called the enthalpy change of the reaction and is given the symbol ∆H. The enthalpy change is the amount of heat energy taken in or given out in a chemical reaction. It is the difference between the energy of the products and the energy of the reactants.

items.label: text
items.text: ∆H is given a minus or a plus sign to show whether heat is being given out or absorbed by the reaction. You always look at it from the point of view of the reactants. For an exothermic reaction, ∆H is given a negative number because the reactants are losing energy as heat. That heat is transferred to the surroundings, which then get warmer. ∆H is measured in units of kJ/mol (kilojoules per mole).

items.label: text
items.text: In an equation, the amount of heat given out or taken in can be shown as, for example:

items.label: text
items.text: The ∆H written next to an equation represents the enthalpy change of the reaction, i.e. 466.9 kJ of heat is given out when one mole of magnesium reacts in this way. You know heat has been given out because ∆H has a negative sign.

items.label: text
items.text: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings is said to be endothermic. If you hold a test-tube in which an endothermic reaction is occurring you will notice that it gets colder.
